phonemes.desc: Lateral affricate [tɬ] plus long open [aː]; tl- is a single Nahuatl initial, and ā marks vowel length.
Voiceless alveolar stop [t] plus long close-mid [eː], the honorific or lordly element.
Voiceless velar stop [k] plus rounded [we], then lateral affricate [tɬ] plus close front [i]; -cuhtli is the reverential suffix meaning 'lord.'

pronunciation.approximation: 'TLAH-lteh-KWEH-tlee' — begin with the single 'tl' sound, hold the first and second vowels long, and treat the final -tl as one release.

kin.label: Nahuatl earth powers
kin.form: Cōātlīcue, Tōnantzin, and Tlāloc share overlapping chthonic and agricultural domains

kin.label: Modern spelling
kin.form: Tlaltecuhtli, the conventional form without vowel-length marking

pronunciation.note: The name is a straightforward compound of tlālli ('earth') and tēcuhtli ('lord'). The honorific suffix is not gender-exclusive in Nahuatl; Tlāltēcuhtli is depicted as both male and female, and sometimes as a toad-like being. Tier 1: the macrons on ā and ē preserve reconstructed vowel length.

domains.title: Lord of the Earth
domains.subtitle: Chthonic Power and Cosmic Sustenance
domains.lead: Tlāltēcuhtli is the living earth beneath the feet of the Fifth Sun, the monster-toad whose body became the world and whose gaping mouth swallows the sun each evening. Unlike the sky gods who demand attention with thunder and light, Tlāltēcuhtli works in silence: receiving the dead, pushing up crops, and reminding mortals that every step is taken on a conscious being.

cards.name: The Earth as Body
cards.desc: Mountains rise from Tlāltēcuhtli's back; rivers flow from its folds; caves are its open mouth.

cards.name: Receiver of the Dead
cards.desc: The sun descends into Tlāltēcuhtli's jaws at sunset; corpses return to the earth that fed them.

cards.name: Agricultural Generosity
cards.desc: Maize, beans, squash, and cotton rise from its body; offerings of blood ensure the earth's continued fruitfulness.

cards.name: Devourer and Transformer
cards.desc: The earth consumes and renews; Tlāltēcuhtli is both tomb and womb, endings and beginnings.

symbols.name: Crouching toad
symbols.meaning: The common posture of Tlāltēcuhtli images, expressing the earth as a low, wide, waiting creature

symbols.name: Gaping jaws
symbols.meaning: The mouth that receives the setting sun and the bodies of the dead

symbols.name: Curved fangs and claws
symbols.meaning: Predatory features that mark the earth's power to destroy as well as nourish

symbols.name: Blood-red coloring
symbols.meaning: Aztec depictions often paint Tlāltēcuhtli red, the color of vitality and sacrifice

mythology.lead: Tlāltēcuhtli appears in several Mesoamerican creation accounts as the earth monster who must be defeated and dismembered before the present world can exist. The most detailed Nahuatl version survives in the Histoyre du Méchique, a sixteenth-century colonial manuscript; the Leyenda de los Soles and the Florentine Codex supply parallel doctrines. These sources are fragmentary and written after the conquest — the tradition itself says so, and this temple reports them as such.

myths.title: The Dismemberment of the Earth Monster
myths.text: Our fullest Nahua creation account survives in a sixteenth-century French manuscript, the Histoyre du Méchique (associated with the cosmographer André Thevet) — colonial, fragmentary, and precious for exactly that reason. It tells that the gods Quetzalcōātl and Tēzcatlīpōca, seeing a great monster in the form of a caiman called Tlāltēcuhtli floating on the primordial waters, transformed themselves into two great serpents and seized her, one by the right hand and foot, one by the left, and tore her in two. From one half they made the earth, from the other the sky; from her hair they made trees, plants, and flowers, from her eyes wells and springs, from her nose rivers and valleys, from her shoulders mountains. The victim did not die quietly: she cried out in the night for the hearts of men, and the gods consented to feed her. The Leyenda de los Soles tells a parallel creation. The myth's meaning is contract, not conquest: the world exists because a being was broken, and it keeps existing only while the debt of flesh is paid.

myths.title: The Sun's Nightly Journey
myths.text: The Florentine Codex — the encyclopedia compiled under Bernardino de Sahagún from Nahua elders in the 1540s–1570s — describes the sun's nightly passage in the plainest physical terms: at evening the sun enters the gaping mouth of the earth in the west, passes through the body of Tlāltēcuhtli, and is delivered again at dawn in the east. To the sources this is no metaphor: the earth has a mouth, jaws, and hunger, and the day itself is a meal it cannot be allowed to refuse. Nahuatl vocabulary underwrites the image — the earth is tlālli, and Tlāltēcuhtli is that land made lord. The doctrine that night is the sun passing through a body made every evening an act of digestion and every morning a birth: in this cosmology time does not flow above the world but through it, and the calendar keeps its count in the gut of the ground.

myths.title: Offerings to the Hungry Earth
myths.text: Sahagún's informants describe a relationship of payment. Before a house was built, a field planted, or a body buried, the earth was addressed and fed — food, flowers, copal incense, and in the highest rites blood — because unfed earth refuses its function (Florentine Codex, Books 1 and 11; Durán, Book of the Gods and Rites). The Codex Magliabechiano illustrates precisely such offerings set before a crouching earth figure. The archaeological correlate is overwhelming: the Templo Mayor excavations have recovered dedicatory caches buried as gifts to the earth at every stage of construction, some containing the remains of sacrifice. Colonial friars read this as devil-worship; the Nahua informants present it as ordinary courtesy. Both testify to the same theology: the ground under Mexico City was never inert — it was a creditor holding the mortgage on every foundation stone.

myths.title: The Red Monolith Beneath the Cathedral
myths.text: On 2 October 2006, in a trench at the foot of the Templo Mayor, Leonardo López Luján's team uncovered a slab that made international news: a monolithic Tlāltēcuhtli more than four metres across, carved crouching with claws extended, a skull at the waist-buckle, death's eyes in its sockets, and traces of red and yellow pigment still in the stone. López Luján associated the monument with the nearby cremation deposits of Mexica rulers — above all Ahuitzotl, who died in 1502 — reading it as the earth lord summoned to receive a king. The find completed a five-hundred-year symmetry: the colonial city was built over the earth's face, its cathedral stones cut from the temples of the precinct; the excavation put the face back into the light. The earth, the Aztecs said, always gets what it is owed — even if payment comes in the currency of archaeology, and five centuries late.

lore.syncretism: Tlāltēcuhtli overlaps with Cōātlīcue, Tōnantzin, and other female earth figures in Nahuatl religion; the gender and precise identity of the earth lord were fluid across regions and periods. In Maya traditions the cognate figure is often the crocodilian earth monster whose body supports the sky. Colonial Christian writers interpreted the earth devourer as a demonic figure, but the persistence of earth shrines and offerings suggests a deeper continuity of chthonic devotion, folded after the conquest into reverence for the land itself and, in the modern period, into an indigenous ecological theology that reads the earth as a living, conscious body.
lore.culturalLegacy: Tlāltēcuhtli entered global consciousness through the vivid monolith discovered during the Templo Mayor excavations in Mexico City — a massive red-painted stone slab showing the crouching, fanged earth lord. The image has become a staple of museum exhibitions on Aztec cosmology and a touchstone for discussions of ecological reciprocity in pre-Columbian thought. Contemporary Mesoamericanist artists and environmental writers invoke Tlāltēcuhtli to express the idea of the earth as a living, conscious, and hungry body.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Every civilization needs a name for the ground it stands on. Tlāltēcuhtli is one of the most direct: 'Lord of the Earth.' But the name is not a title of ownership; it is a title of relation. The earth is not property but a being with jaws, with hunger, with the power to refuse. To walk on Tlāltēcuhtli is to incur a debt.

The image of the sun swallowed each evening and reborn each morning is one of the oldest visual metaphors in Mesoamerica. It teaches that nothing is lost, only transformed. The corpse becomes soil, the soil becomes maize, the maize becomes blood, the blood becomes prayer. Tlāltēcuhtli is the still center of that wheel, the being who receives everything and returns everything, at a price.

lore.archaeology: The most spectacular find is the monolithic Tlāltēcuhtli sculpture uncovered in 2006 near the Templo Mayor, measuring more than 4 meters on a side and preserving red and yellow pigment. Templo Mayor excavations have located Tlāltēcuhtli shrines, offering caches, and sculptural reliefs showing the sun entering the earth's mouth. Postclassic and early colonial pictorial manuscripts such as the Codex Borgia and Codex Magliabechiano preserve ritual and iconographic details of the earth lord.
